name: Pheromone sprays (Human Pheromone Sciences)

lead: These are fragrance products sold on the claim that they contain human sex pheromones.
Expert reviews report no peer-reviewed demonstration that human pheromones affect behavior.

paras: Proponents say pheromone compounds signal attraction; researchers note human pheromone function has not been conclusively shown.
No specific harms were found in the sources reviewed; main concern cited is lack of supporting evidence.

lead: Pheromone sprays are commercial fragrance products marketed as containing human sex pheromones that increase attractiveness. Human Pheromone Sciences is named as a seller of such products.

Researchers report that no pheromonal substance has been shown in peer-reviewed studies to directly influence human behavior, describing the field as speculative and controversial.[1] The studies listed in the entry's source search concern insect pheromones, not humans.[2]
infobox: Not supported by peer-reviewed human studies[1]

paras: Reported findings include androstenol and androstadienone studies on perception and attention, menstrual synchrony claims later questioned, and MHC-linked odor preferences.[1] Reviewers cite small samples, publication bias and poor methodology, and note the human vomeronasal organ receptor genes are nonfunctional pseudogenes.[1]
Advertisers claim body sprays contain human sexual pheromones acting as an aphrodisiac; the claims are described as not supported by peer-reviewed evidence.[1]
No studies found of these commercial products. Pheromone spray research located concerns insects such as codling moths and honey bees.[2]
